clinicalPearls: First-degree block is a fixed PR prolongation with every P wave conducted, whereas third-degree block shows complete atrioventricular dissociation with an independent escape rhythm.
Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat and usually reflects reversible block within the atrioventricular node.
Mobitz type II block shows constant PR intervals with sudden non-conducted P waves and localises to the His-Purkinje system, carrying a high risk of progression to complete block.
A narrow escape complex suggests a junctional pacemaker with a relatively reliable rate, while a wide, slow escape indicates a ventricular pacemaker that is more likely to fail.
The level of block, rather than the numerical degree alone, drives prognosis and the decision to pace.
In 2 to 1 block the type cannot be classified by the PR pattern, so accompanying QRS width and response to vagal or exercise manoeuvres help localise the level.
Vagal tone slows the sinus rate and improves nodal (Wenckebach) block but worsens infranodal block, whereas exercise or atropine does the reverse, a useful bedside distinction.
Reversible causes such as ischaemia, drugs including AV-nodal blockers, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism, Lyme disease and raised vagal tone should be excluded before permanent pacing.
reference.pathophysiology: Atrioventricular block denotes impaired conduction of the atrial impulse to the ventricles, which may be delayed, intermittently interrupted or completely blocked. The site of disease determines the clinical behaviour. Block within the atrioventricular node is typically decremental, often vagally mediated or drug-related, and tends to produce Wenckebach periodicity with a stable junctional escape. Block within the His-Purkinje system is an all-or-none phenomenon reflecting diffuse conduction-system disease, and it generates Mobitz type II or complete block with an unreliable, slow ventricular escape. Causes span idiopathic age-related fibrosis of the conduction system, ischaemia and infarction, infiltrative and inflammatory disease, congenital block associated with maternal anti-Ro antibodies, drugs, electrolyte disturbance and increased vagal tone.

redFlags: syncope or presyncope with documented high-grade or complete block
Mobitz type II or complete block with a wide, slow or unstable escape rhythm
block complicating acute anterior myocardial infarction
alternating bundle branch block indicating advanced conduction-system disease
reference.prognosis: First-degree and Mobitz type I block are usually benign when asymptomatic and reversible causes are addressed, whereas Mobitz type II and complete infranodal block frequently progress and warrant permanent pacing, after which prognosis is largely determined by the underlying cardiac disease. Congenital complete block may be tolerated for years but often eventually requires pacing.
pitfalls: Classifying 2 to 1 block as type I or type II from the conduction ratio alone rather than from QRS width and provocative manoeuvres.
Missing reversible causes such as drug effect, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism or Lyme carditis before implanting a permanent device.
Mistaking blocked atrial premature beats for genuine second-degree block.
Underestimating the danger of Mobitz type II because the resting rate appears adequate.
Overlooking that vagal manoeuvres improve nodal but worsen infranodal block when trying to localise the level.

management: Identify and reverse contributory causes, withdrawing atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs and correcting electrolyte disturbance, ischaemia, hypothyroidism or Lyme disease
Observe asymptomatic first-degree and Mobitz type I block without pacing when reversible causes have been addressed
Implant a permanent pacemaker for symptomatic bradycardia and for high-risk infranodal disease such as Mobitz type II or complete heart block
Stabilise acute symptomatic or haemodynamically compromising block with atropine, isoprenaline and temporary transcutaneous or transvenous pacing as a bridge to definitive therapy
Monitor with inpatient telemetry to capture intermittent high-grade block and treat the underlying structural or ischaemic heart disease
Refer congenital complete block associated with maternal anti-Ro antibodies for specialist paediatric cardiology care
